'''''Nigella damascena''''', '''love-in-a-mist''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref>  or '''devil in the bush''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=NIDA|taxon=Nigella damascena|accessdate=20 July 2015}}</ref> is an [[Annual plant|annual]] garden [[flowering plant]], belonging to the buttercup [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Ranunculaceae]]. 
It is [[native plant|native]] to southern Europe (but [[Adventive species|adventive]] in more northern countries of Europe), north Africa and southwest Asia, where it is found on neglected, damp patches of land.

The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''damascena'' relates to [[Damascus]] in Syria.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref> The plant's common name "love-in-a-mist" comes from the flower being nestled in a ring of [[wikt:multifid|multifid]], lacy [[bract]]s.

==Description==
It grows to {{convert|20|-|50|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall, with pinnately divided, thread-like,  alternate [[leaf|leaves]]. The [[flower]]s, blooming in early summer, are most commonly different shades of blue, but can be white, pink, or pale purple, with 5 to 25 [[sepal]]s. The actual [[petal]]s are located at the base of the stamens and are minute and clawed. The sepals are the only colored part of the [[perianth]]. The four to five [[carpel]]s of the compound [[pistil]] have each an erect [[carpel|style]].<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book | editor-last = Brickell | editor-first = Christopher | title = The Royal Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants | year = 2008 | page = 726 | publisher = Dorling Kindersley | location = United Kingdom | isbn = 9781405332965}}</ref>

The [[fruit]] is a large and inflated [[Capsule (fruit)|capsule]], growing from a compound [[ovary (plants)|ovary]], and is  composed of several united follicles, each containing numerous [[seed]]s. This is rather exceptional for a member of the buttercup family. The capsule becomes brown in late summer. The plant self-seeds, growing on the same spot year after year.<ref name = EOL>{{cite web 
| url = http://eol.org/pages/596373/details | title = ''Nigella damascena'' | publisher = Encyclopedia of Life 
| accessdate = 13 April 2018}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Nigella damascena.jpg|thumb|Selection of cultivars]]
This easily  grown plant has been a familiar subject in English [[cottage garden]]s since Elizabethan times, admired for its ferny foliage, spiky flowers and bulbous seed-heads.  It is now widely cultivated throughout the [[temperateness|temperate]] world, and numerous [[cultivars]] have been developed for garden use. 'Persian Jewels' is a mixture of white, pink, lavender and blue flowers. 'Persian Rose' is pale pink. Other [[cultivar]]s are 'Albion', 'Blue Midget', 'Cambridge Blue', 'Mulberry Rose', and 'Oxford Blue'. 'Dwarf Moody Blue' is around {{convert|15|cm|0|abbr=on}} high. The pale blue ‘Miss Jekyll’<ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/106194/i-Nigella-damascena-i-Miss-Jekyll/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Nigella damascena'' 'Miss Jekyll' | accessdate = 13 April 2018}}</ref> and the double white-flowered 'Miss Jekyll Alba' have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Nigella damascena'' 'Miss Jekyll Alba'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/106195/Nigella-damascena-Miss-Jekyll-Alba/Details | accessdate=23 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 69 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 13 April 2018}}</ref>

==Related species==
The related ''[[Nigella sativa]]'' (and not ''N. damascena'') is the source of the spice variously known as nigella, ''kalonji'' or black cumin.

==Toxicity==
[[Damascenine]] is a toxic [[alkaloid]] found in ''Nigella damascena'' seed.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Margout|first1=Delphine|last2=Kelly|first2=Mary T.|last3=Meunier|first3=Sylvie|last4=Auinger|first4=Doris|last5=Pelissier|first5=Yves|last6=Larroque|first6=Michel|title=Morphological, microscopic and chemical comparison between Nigella sativa L. cv (black cumin) and Nigella damascena L. cv|journal=Journal of Food, Agriculture and Environment|date=2013|volume=11|issue=1|pages=132–138|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/250002686}}</ref>

However, an [[in vivo]] study in mice (100 ppm i.p.) and [[In vitro toxicology|in vitro]] assessment on human cell lines has not shown any toxicity.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Damascenine induced hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity in mice and in vitro assessed human erythrocyte toxicity|first1=Yacine|last1=Bouguezza|first2=Bachra|last2=Khettal|first3=Lydia|last3=Tir|first4=Souad|last4=Boudrioua|date=September 2, 2015|journal=Interdisciplinary Toxicology|volume=8|issue=3|pages=118–124|doi=10.1515/intox-2015-0018|pmid=27486370|pmc=4961907}}</ref>
